items.title: Egypt calls for Yemen talks as parliament weighs military support to Saudi Arabia
items.summary: Egypt calls for Yemen talks as parliament weighs military support to Saudi Arabia Egypt advocates exploring "every opportunity" to resolve the Yemen war diplomatically, its foreign minister said, ahead of a parliamentary vote next week on authorising the armed forces to support Saudi Arabia against the Iran-aligned Houthis. Any direct involvement of the Egyptian military, one of the region's largest, would raise the stakes in the fighting between the kingdom and the Houthis, an increasingly destabilising front in the spreading US-Israeli war on Iran. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi called on Saturday for an urgent parliamentary session to authorise military involvement supporting the kingdom. After a closed session on Sunday, lawmakers postponed the vote until 26 October to allow more deliberation. Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and intelligence chief Hassan Rashad travelled to Riyadh on Wednesday to deliver a letter from Sisi to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

items.title: European Parliament calls for Houthi terrorist listing
items.summary: LONDON: The European Parliament called on Thursday for the Houthi militia in Yemen to be included on the EU’s list of terrorist organizations. MEPs overwhelmingly backed a resolution that said the Iran-backed group’s military and political wings, leadership, and military and security apparatus, should be designated. The text called for all channels of financing for the Houthis to be dismantled and for the EU to freeze funds and economic resources belonging to the group and its facilitators.

items.title: Impact of Houthi attacks on Saudi economy 'limited' for now: IMF
items.summary: Impact of Houthi attacks on Saudi economy 'limited' for now: IMF Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are having only a "limited" economic impact on the kingdom so far, owing to robust domestic demand, the IMF's regional director told AFP, though geopolitical uncertainty remains a threat. The Iranian-backed Yemeni group has ramped up its attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, hitting oil facilities and airports among other targets, as Yemen's dormant civil war has roared back into life. The world's largest oil exporter, Saudi Arabia, has had its crude shipments squeezed by Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthis' declaration of a maritime blockade. But shipments continue to move despite the conflicts, Jihad Azour told AFP.

items.summary: Turkey warns against renewed attack on Iran, says diplomacy only way Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan cautioned on Friday against any renewed attack on Iran, saying such a move would exacerbate tensions and further expand the conflict. Diplomacy and dialogue are the only way to end the war, Fidan told the press after meeting with foreign ministers from Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Germany, France, Britain and Italy. "A military intervention on Iran is not in any way a solution. Nobody approves this at the moment," he added. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot also said after Friday's meetings that renewed escalation between Iran and the United States would only have losers and raise oil prices. items.summary: IRGC says three tankers hit mines crossing Hormuz Strait Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Tuesday that its naval mines halted three tankers attempting to travel the Strait of Hormuz via routes considered illegal by Tehran. "Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted due to the explosion of mines planted by the brave sailors of the IRGC Navy at an illegal crossing point in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz," the IRGC said in a statement on its official Sepah News website. The Guard later said in a statement carried by state TV that a third oil tanker "exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz". The statement added that the tanker, "carrying over 2 million barrels of crude oil, had deactivated all of its radar and navigation systems".

items.title: UN Security Council condemns 'escalatory' Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia
items.summary: UN Security Council condemns 'escalatory' Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia The UN Security Council has condemned the "escalatory" attacks by Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi Arabia, including "reckless strikes" on Riyadh's airport. The Saudi capital's international airport has been targeted by strikes 20 times since the beginning of the month, with an attack last weekend killing 13 people and wounding more than 300. In a joint statement shared by the Security Council's president, Greece's Evangelos Sekeris, the 15-member UN body also condemned "continued Houthi attacks and threats against commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab (Strait)". The statement also "affirmed the inherent right of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia of self-defence in accordance with international law."

items.summary: From his shop in south Lebanon near the Israeli border, Mark Diab says life in his village will be turned upside down when a decades-long United Nations peacekeeping force pulls out next year. "UNIFIL isn't just business, to us it's family," said Diab, 59, whose sister is among residents of Ibl al-Saqi who have married peacekeepers from the UN Interim Force in Lebanon over the years. She now lives in Spain. "We're basically open because of the UN. We started when I was young," Diab said from his shop, just down the road from a UNIFIL base, selling clothes.

items.title: As Trump’s time runs out, this could be his most dangerous legacy: a world divided into three | Steve Bloomfield
items.summary: We’ve heard much about the end of the west. At the proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, those fears could crystallise In the final two years of a US presidency, when Congress has been lost, approval ratings have sunk like a stone and their party has started to think about who’s coming next, the person occupying the Oval Office can feel their power draining away. Domestic legislation, particularly in an era where bipartisan cooperation is almost nonexistent, grinds to a halt. But as the days tick by until the end, and as presidents begin to think about their legacy, there is one part of the job where they still have power: the rest of the world. In the final weeks of his presidency in 1992 George HW Bush sent 28,000 American troops to Somalia to help end a famine. For Bill Clinton, it was a quixotic attempt to bring peace to the Middle East by ending the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. "We could end it very quickly," Trump said. "Do we want to finish it off or just want to let it wither?" Speaking to reporters on the White House South Lawn before departing for Florida, Trump said oil was passing through the Strait of Hormuz. "We are getting everything we want,” he said. items.summary: ‘Turkey is a common enemy’: Pro-Israel network forms parliamentary groups in Greece and Cyprus Pro- Israel US lobby group Aipac has visited Cyprus to promote what it called “security partnerships in the Eastern Mediterranean” between Israel, Cyprus and the US. The delegation , led by outgoing Aipac president Bernard Kaminetsky and president-elect Yehuda Neuberger, met President Nikos Christodoulides on Wednesday, underscoring Cyprus’s growing importance to Israeli interests. Aipac faces widespread condemnation in the US for its influence over members of Congress and US presidents and for pushing an Israel-first agenda, including backing the war on Iran, which has caused global economic fallout. The meeting came just days after another pro-Israel lobby group with far-right links, the Israel Allies Foundation (IAF), launched parliamentary caucuses in Greece and Cyprus to deepen Israel’s influence in both countries’ parliaments. clusters.headline: Ahead of US and Israeli elections, 3-day joint attack on Iran 'would not radically change conflict'

items.title: Ahead of US and Israeli elections, 3-day joint attack on Iran 'would not radically change conflict'
items.summary: Jean-Emile Jammine is pleased to welcome Federico Donelli, Associate Professor of International Relations in the Department of Political and Social Sciences at the University of Trieste in Italy. Can another three days of military strikes achieve what eight months of confrontation have failed to deliver? Donelli challenges the assumption that a short, intensive offensive would necessarily produce a decisive political outcome. He argues, "the real question is whether military pressure is intended to constrain Iran's capacity, or to pressure Iran to sit on the table." And whether they can translate that capacity into a sustainable political outcome without provoking a wider regional crisis. Regardless, Donelli reminds us that "Iran still has leverage over the US."

Het hof staat onder zware druk van de Verenigde Staten . President Trump wil met sancties het hof platleggen. "Met de toekenning van de prijs aan het Strafhof erkent het Europarlement het belangrijke werk van het hof bij het handhaven van het internationaal recht en de internationale rechtspraak", zegt parlementsvoorzitter Roberta Metsola. Wat doet het Internationaal Strafhof? Het Strafhof onderzoekt, vervolgt en berecht personen die worden beschuldigd van mensenrechtenschendingen en dient als aanvulling op de nationale rechtbanken van aangesloten landen. Het hof doet onder meer onderzoek naar genocide, oorlogsmisdaden en misdaden tegen de menselijkheid. Alle landen in de Europese Unie zijn verplicht om besluiten van het Strafhof uit te voeren, vanwege het Statuut van Rome. Het hof wordt niet door alle landen in de wereld erkend. Zo erkennen de VS, Israël, Rusland en Iran het hof niet. Het Strafhof, dat volgend jaar met sancties vanuit de VS te maken kr

items.title: Was the MOU meant to be trashed?
items.summary: As President Trump appeared to accept an end to the Iran war by agreeing to the short-lived Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on June 17, many Republican senators were deeply alarmed. Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) openly trashed the agreement, warning Ronald Reagan was “ rolling over in his grave ,” before getting into a war of words with President Donald Trump over the administration’s strategy. Yet opposition to the MOU with Iran abruptly softened. Cassidy received a briefing from Vice President JD Vance and Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff that convinced him to flip his votes on future war powers resolutions on Iran. He suggested afterwards that the administration had a “ plausible plan ” to accomplish many of the war’s original goals to destroy or degrade Iran’s nuclear program, ballistic missiles and conventional warfare capabilities. items.summary: American farmers are in crisis, facing rising costs, disrupted export markets, and mounting financial pressure. While farming has always faced unavoidable challenges, such as weather, pests, and the vagaries of demand, the present problems are entirely of Washington’s making. The Trump administration’s tariffs have damaged critical trading relations, and its war against Iran has disrupted energy and fertilizer trade through the Strait of Hormuz. Washington’s response to beleaguered American agricultural interests has been billions of dollars in emergency aid and promises that future trade deals will deliver additional relief. It is a familiar cycle: Washington creates new risks for American producers, taxpayers absorb part of the resulting losses, and the underlying policies remain in place. Farmers receive temporary assistance but are left to navigate the same uncertain markets and elevated costs that made the assistance necessary. items.summary: Abito scuro e cravatta rossa d'ordinanza: Donald Trump si agita dietro le sbarre di una cella sospesa sul traffico di piazza Tajrish, a Teheran. Non è intelligenza artificiale ma una nuova provocazione iraniana: l’installazione, promossa dall’organizzazione municipale che cura gli spazi urbani della capitale, chiude la campagna “Non vedere questa scena è un crimine”, costruita per ricordare le vittime iraniane del conflitto e invocare la punizione dei responsabili. I passanti si fermano, ridono, insultano il finto presidente americano e riprendono la scena con i cellulari. Tutto ciò arriva mentre i rapporti tra Washington e Teheran sono nuovamente in stallo. Trump ha respinto il piano iraniano per riaprire lo Stretto di Hormuz e fermare le ostilità, sostenendo che Teheran voglia un accordo perché “sta perdendo”; successivamente ha assicurato che gli Stati Uniti non avrebbero sferrato nuovi attacchi prima delle elezioni di metà mandato del 3 novembre. items.title: The Guardian view on the Republicans’ midterms struggle: Trump has circuses, but voters also want bread | Editorial
items.summary: As prices keep rising, more of the president’s supporters are asking what happened to the economic good times he promised It is no great revelation that Donald Trump is enriching himself as president. He raked in $2.2bn in 2025, with his position and his personal interests frequently overlapping. Yet this week’s poll finding that 34% of Republicans (and 66% of all American voters) think that he is using his position to make himself rich merits attention . Separately, voters in a Fox News poll last week put government corruption at the top of their list of concerns – just ahead of inflation and high prices. Mr Trump pledged that people would be better off if they voted for him. Billionaires are; not the rest. He promised to lower grocery costs (they have risen) and to cut the price of gasoline to below $2 a gallon. It’s more than double that, thanks to his illegal war on Iran. Tariffs haven’t helped. items.summary: Iraq orders Sheeb crossing into Iran closed as more shutdowns loom Two sources at Iraq's Sheeb crossing into Iran told Reuters that officials had halted passenger, vehicle and commercial-truck traffic. They said the crossing was “closed to passengers, vehicles and commercial trucks until further notice”. A separate source told Reuters that authorities made the decision to review security arrangements at the crossing. An Iraqi government source earlier told Al Jazeera that the government had ordered the closure but gave no reason. The source said Iraq would gradually close several more crossings with Iran in the coming days. Officials have not issued a public statement or said how many crossings they plan to close.

items.title: Death toll from Houthi strike on Yemen government camp rises to 73
items.summary: Death toll from Houthi strike on Yemen government camp rises to 73 Local Yemeni authorities on Tuesday raised the death toll from a Houthi strike a day earlier on a military camp belonging to government forces to 73, as fighting between the foes escalates. It marked the deadliest attack in weeks as fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognised, Saudi-supported government rages after the collapse of a years-long truce. The death toll from Monday's strike on the camp in the energy-rich Shabwa province "increased to 73 martyrs, while search and follow-up efforts are ongoing to discover the fate of 14 missing people", authorities said in a statement. Local authorities had put the death toll at 53 on Monday, adding that more than 200 others were injured, all new members of the internal security forces who were undergoing training.

items.summary: A plurality of active-duty service members — 48% — oppose the military being used in the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, according to a poll conducted by Change Research for the advocacy group Common Defense. The poll surveyed 156 people currently serving in the military, 431 veterans, and  144 immediate family members of active-duty service members between September 15 and 28. Nearly 20% identified as “pure independents,” while 35% said they were Democrats. Though Republicans surveyed in the poll backed Operation Epic Fury at a rate of 77% to 16%, overwhelming opposition among Democrats and independents left respondents opposed to the war overall, 49% to 44%. items.title: How the UAE and MEK weaponize AI to spread propaganda
items.summary: Somewhere inside Iran, a network of activists exchanged messages about politics and news with an activist — nicknamed “Parsa” — on the messaging app Telegram. They had no idea they were actually speaking to an AI agent that had copied the real activist’s style by training it on 8,400 real Telegram posts. Instead of “Parsa,” they were actually communicating with the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran (MEK), an Iranian Islamist-Marxist opposition group widely regarded as a cult. According to a report from Anthropic released last month, this operation was carried out by four individuals working for the MEK. They built an AI agent named “Viktor” that also surveilled individuals inside Iran and flooded social media platforms with pro-MEK content under “independent” branding. The Anthropic report sheds light on how foreign actors are increasingly using artificial intelligence tools like Claude and ChatGPT for their influence operations. items.title: As Houthis encircle Taiz, Yemen's Saudi-backed gov't faces disaster
items.summary: Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, endured a siege from 2015 to 2017. Today, it is encircled again. The World Food Program says it cannot reach more than 600,000 people in and around the city. The International Organization for Migration counts over 200,000 people displaced since the Houthi offensive on Yemen’s Red Sea coast launched in September. Why this city, and why now? The Houthis, formally known as the Ansar Allah movement, draw their strength from the Zaydi Shia highlands of the north. Critics say their governing ideology rests on the belief that the right to rule belongs to sayyids , descendants of the Prophet Mohammad, a lineage to which the Houthi family itself belongs. The Houthis have long denied seeking to restore the Imamate, but in Taiz, which has for a decade resisted Houthi encroachment, that denial finds few believers. Taiz has a long history of political activism and hostility to the idea of religious hereditary rule. items.title: The Fog of Tech
items.summary: Mara Karlin, a defense policy expert who served as senior national-security official in multiple American administrations, makes an authoritative case that war planners tend to be overconfident about their ability to predict how new tools will shape the battlefield—blinding them to the unchanging realities of war. Using examples from Gaza, Ukraine, and Iran, Karlin shows how this "technology trap" leads to false assumptions about the future of war.

clusters.headline: Maritime Chokepoints: Hormuz and Beyond

items.title: Maritime Chokepoints: Hormuz and Beyond
items.summary: Iran did not need a navy to close the Strait of Hormuz and disrupt global trade – only missiles on shore, drones in the air, and mines beneath the waves. For centuries, only naval power could determine who used the world's narrow straits, but now even navy-less actors can disrupt global trade. To keep the sea lanes open, America and its allies must deter attempts to close a chokepoint and build the reserves and bypass routes that blunt the damage when narrow waterways do close.

items.summary: Iran’s attacks on Hormuz shipping 'unsuccessful', Centcom says The US military says the “vast majority” of Iran’s attempted attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz have failed, and that the waterway remains open. On Saturday, US Central Command spokesperson Tim Hawkins told Fox News that about 97 percent of vessels trying to cross the strait had done so without being struck, many of them with US military protection. “What the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of Iran is doing is unjustified and it’s also unsuccessful because they are not achieving their objective of closing the Strait of Hormuz,” Hawkins said.

items.title: Hormuz controlled by US and allies, not Iran: Centcom chief
items.summary: Hormuz controlled by US and allies, not Iran: Centcom chief The Strait of Hormuz "is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran ", the head of US Central Command (Centcom) has said. In a video statement, Centcom commander Brad Cooper said the US blockade of Iranian ports had imposed "a devastating cost" on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). He said it had completely halted Iran's maritime exports and imports, "with the exception of humanitarian assistance we have allowed in". Cooper said the US had "prevented Iran from exporting at least 25 billion dollars worth of crude oil" and had "significantly degraded Iran's ability to project power far beyond its borders". He added that US forces had helped Gulf allies ship more than 100 million barrels of crude through the strait in the past week, with around 400 merchant vessels passing through. In total, the US had helped regional partners move 1.3 billion barrels through Hormuz in recent months, he said.

Spain’s parliament had approved a package worth more than 12 billion euros ($13.4bn) “to protect the affected sectors and also to protect citizens who use their cars”. items.title: US weighs lifting sanctions on Iran's 'shadow fleet' to address surging costs
items.summary: US weighs lifting sanctions on Iran's 'shadow fleet' to address surging costs The US is considering lifting sanctions on “shadow fleet” tankers tied to Russia and Iran to address soaring diesel prices ahead of midterm elections, according to multiple reports and a senior US official. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a video address to an energy forum in Riyadh this week that the Trump administration was discussing easing sanctions on shadow fleet vessels to address record freight rates that have driven up costs of shipping American energy abroad, Energy Aspects, a research group, said. The Financial Times reported on Thursday that the US could allow the sale of blacklisted vessels to non-sanctioned operators and lift sanctions, allowing them to operate without restrictions. Reuters reported the US could allow “legal oil" to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, effectively allowing sanctioned ships to carry crude or petroleum products not sanctioned by the US. items.title: La poesía no ha muerto
items.summary: Dice Andrés Trapiello que la poesía no ha muerto, esto es que vive, pero no así el mundo que la necesitaba. Lo dice, a su manera, para celebrar un aniversario de la editorial La Veleta, que el escritor fundó hace ahora cien libros de poemas, después de otras aventuras editoriales, como Trieste. Y lo celebra con la publicación de las traducciones de Emily Dickinson que debemos a Carlos Pujol, lector y traductor y persona inmejorable. Que el mundo haya necesitado la poesía alguna vez es una interesante hipótesis que muchos hechos podrían desmentir. O muchos versos: la flor que el arado destroza en el poema de Catulo, las cuatro personas para las que escribía Pound (¡oh mundo, lo siento por ti!), la tumba en el aire que excavan los judíos de la ‘Fuga de la muerte’ de Celan, o el combatiente ejecutado ante los ojos de René Char, caído como una hoja que una ráfaga de viento arrastraría... O la misma ausencia que Omar Jayyam mostró a la Luna hace mil años desde un huerto en el Jorasán iraní: ‘Cuantas y cuantas veces volverás a buscarme en el mismo jardín y todo será inútil’. Zijn land staat aan de vooravond van een zware winter en de vrees is dat Rusland zal proberen om de Oekraïense energiesector nog harder te raken. Onder meer de hoofdstad Kyiv wordt dagelijks aangevallen met ballistische raketten en de voorraad Patriot-raketten om die projectielen tegen te houden is zo goed als op . items.summary: Los rebeldes hutíes no cesan su ofensiva contra el Gobierno de Yemen y sus aliados en la región. Su último golpe ha sido un ataque con misiles contra el palacio presidencial yemení en la ciudad portuaria de Adén, al sur del país. El impacto dejó cinco muertos y, al menos, 16 heridos.Los hutíes, una guerrilla chií aliada de Irán, llevan varias semanas de ofensiva contra las tropas del Ejército regular de Yemen y también contra su vecino, Arabia Saudí. El primer ministro yemení, Shaya Zindani, calificó el ataque como un gesto «cobarde» de los hutíes que no hace más que recalcar «la continuación de su comportamiento criminal». clusters.headline: Voters more worried about Iran war than immigration or crime: polls

items.title: Voters more worried about Iran war than immigration or crime: polls
items.summary: As election day nears, two new polls show the Iran war has emerged as one of the most important issues shaping voters’ midterm decisions. National polls from Fox News and The Associated Press-NORC place the war behind only economy-related issues, government corruption, and health care among voters’ top four concerns. Significantly, the Iran war has surpassed immigration and crime, two issues on which President Donald Trump performed particularly well in 2024, among voters’ top concerns. In the 2024 campaign, pre - and post -election polling showed those issues as ranking higher as a priority for voters than foreign policy. The Fox News survey showed 75% of respondents were either “extremely” (42%) or “very” (33%) concerned about the war in Iran. According to the AP-NORC poll , 62% of registered voters named the war as one of the most important issues, and a further 31% said it was “an important issue, but not one of the most important.” The Fox poll further found that six in 10 voters oppose U.S. military action against Iran, and those voters favor Democratic congressional candidates

items.title: Gulf states have downplayed damage caused by Iranian strikes: Report
items.summary: Gulf states have downplayed damage caused by Iranian strikes: Report Arabian Gulf monarchies have “suppressed” information about the extent of damage done to their physical infrastructure by attacks from Iran and its allies, Reuters reported on Thursday. Gulf states such as Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, and Kuwait faced thousands of missile and drone strikes launched by Iran in retaliation for the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic on 28 February. More recently, Saudi Arabia has come under attack from the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthis and Iran targeted civilian infrastructure like pipelines, energy facilities and, in one case, a nuclear energy plant. Reuters' assessment is likely to cast new doubt on how Gulf states describe strikes on their territories. For example, Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said that a Houthi drone strike caused a "limited fire" at the headquarters of the kingdom's national oil company, Aramco, in Dhahran. Correspondent Daisy Mohr schetst in podcast De Dag hoe de aanvallen van de Houti's de afgelopen tijd intensiveerden. Veel mensen zullen de strijdgroep kennen van het enteren van containerschepen in de Rode Zee. Maar sinds de oorlog tussen de VS en Iran zijn de mogelijkheden voor de Houthi's uitgebreid. Wie kan hen stoppen? Reageren? Mail naar dedag@nos.nl Presentatie & montage: Marco Geijtenbeek Redactie: Judith van de Hulsbeek en Judith Kutschenreuter

items.title: Chinese refiners rush to buy Middle East crude as stocks fall, Kpler says
items.summary: Chinese refiners rush to buy Middle East crude as stocks fall, Kpler says Chinese refiners are stepping up purchases of Middle Eastern crude as record inventory drawdowns and a recovery in refinery activity boost demand for prompt cargoes, according to analytics firm Kpler. Chinese buyers have secured at least 80 million barrels of Saudi crude since mid-September, Kpler said on X. China’s onshore crude inventories fell by about 1.6 million barrels per day in September, the fastest pace on record. Refinery throughput is projected to reach 14.2 million barrels per day by December, adding to pressure on refiners to rebuild stocks. At the same time, Chinese refiners need to replace roughly 1 million barrels per day of Iranian supply, with the US blockade still in place, according to Kpler. Stronger Chinese demand could limit further weakness in Dubai crude pricing, particularly as escalating regional tensions continue to threaten supply flows.

Op het spel staat een meerderheid in de twee Kamers van het Congres: het Huis van Afgevaardigden en de Senaat. De Republikeinen zetten alles op alles om hun meerderheden te behouden en de Democraten gaan op hun beurt tot het uiterste om die te veroveren. En ze zien een kans: in meerdere staten lijkt volgens de peilingen een verrassing mogelijk. Deze verkiezingen zijn voor Democraten dé mogelijkheid om de macht in Washington weer een beetje naar zich toe te trekken. De afgelopen twee jaar hebben Donald Trump en zijn Republikeinse partij met hun meerderheden in het Congres een stempel op het land en de wereld gedrukt. De acties van de president zijn voor veel mensen een reden om te gaan stemmen bij de midterm elections . Vaak worden tussentijdse verkiezingen gezien als indirect referendum over de president. items.title: As Trump’s time runs out, this could be his most dangerous legacy: a world divided into three | Steve Bloomfield
items.summary: We’ve heard much about the end of the west. At the proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, those fears could crystallise In the final two years of a US presidency, when Congress has been lost, approval ratings have sunk like a stone and their party has started to think about who’s coming next, the person occupying the Oval Office can feel their power draining away. Domestic legislation, particularly in an era where bipartisan cooperation is almost nonexistent, grinds to a halt. But as the days tick by until the end, and as presidents begin to think about their legacy, there is one part of the job where they still have power: the rest of the world. In the final weeks of his presidency in 1992 George HW Bush sent 28,000 American troops to Somalia to help end a famine. For Bill Clinton, it was a quixotic attempt to bring peace to the Middle East by ending the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Barack Obama restored diplomatic ties with Cuba, making a historic visit to Havana, as well as a final, successful push on the Iran nuclear deal. Continue reading...

items.title: Israel's elections and not so great expectations for peace
items.summary: Israelis head to the polls on October 27 in a vote that will cast Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his right-wing and religious allies against a motley crew of opposition parties. At the moment, neither side is expected to have a clear path to the 61-seat majority needed to form a government in the 120-seat Knesset. Netanyahu and his leading opponent are only projected to win some 20 seats each, but the biggest party doesn’t necessarily get the right to form the government. Instead, the Israeli president hands that job to whichever Knesset member has the best shot at winning the Knesset’s confidence. Tuesday’s vote should offer an early indication of which candidate will earn that right. While both main parties in contention advocate continued wars against Hamas and Iran, they differ on key domestic issues as well as their approach to settler violence in the West Bank. items.summary: October sees highest number of ship attacks on record, report says October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017. "October has seen the highest number of ship attacks on record," said Noam Raydan, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. Raydan, who maintains the institute's interactive shipping incident map, has recorded 28 confirmed and reported attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways in October and 113 since the US-Israeli war with Iran began on February 28. The institute's map shows most of the attacks that took place in September and October were in the Strait of Hormuz. The tally broadly aligns with data from the International Maritime Organisation (IMO), which recorded a total of 120 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East since the conflict with Iran began. items.title: Two supertankers using unauthorised Hormuz route hit naval mines, IRGC says
items.summary: Two supertankers using unauthorised Hormuz route hit naval mines, IRGC says Two supertankers struck naval mines while attempting to use an unauthorised route south of the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy said. The ensuing explosions and intense fires left the engine rooms of both vessels disabled, leaving them stranded in the waterway, IRGC said. Fars news agency, meanwhile, cited an IRGC source as saying that Hormuz traffic by violating vessels has come to a halt, following the strikes on three oil tankers on Thursday, destruction of navigation-aid systems on the violating vessels and the destruction of another violating vessel on Thursday night. The source told Fars agency that if oil smuggling resumes, IRGC's response will be "far more forceful". IRGC Navy: Two supertankers in violation attempted to transit the off-limits southern corridor of the Strait of Hormuz. Both vessels struck a naval mine, and following explosions and intense fires, their engine rooms were disabled, leaving them stranded in place. https://t.co/pI0Wd7NeY2 — IRNA News Agency ☫

items.title: Turkey warns against renewed attack on Iran, says diplomacy only way
items.summary: Turkey warns against renewed attack on Iran, says diplomacy only way Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan cautioned on Friday against any renewed attack on Iran, saying such a move would exacerbate tensions and further expand the conflict. Diplomacy and dialogue are the only way to end the war, Fidan told the press after meeting with foreign ministers from Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Germany, France, Britain and Italy. "A military intervention on Iran is not in any way a solution. Nobody approves this at the moment," he added. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot also said after Friday's meetings that renewed escalation between Iran and the United States would only have losers and raise oil prices. items.summary: Iran has plans to target Gulf undersea cables if attacked again, officials say Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel attack Iran again, two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters. Speaking on condition of anonymity, the officials gave few details and did not say how or where Tehran would carry out such attacks. But one of them said Iran would aim to prevent repairs after any attacks to prolong disruptions to communications, including internet connections. "If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines ... from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones," one of the officials said, warning Washington not to "play with fire". The second official said Washington’s Gulf allies, which have invested heavily in such infrastructure, “should hold Washington, not Tehran, responsible for any damage to undersea cables.” Yadollah Javani, the deputy head of political affairs for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said on Wednesday that Iran could target seven major internet cables

items.title: Trump says US could end Iran war quickly or let it 'wither'
items.summary: Trump says US could end Iran war quickly or let it 'wither' US President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington could end the war with Iran quickly, but questioned whether to seek a swift conclusion or let the conflict wind down gradually. "We could end it very quickly," Trump said. "Do we want to finish it off or just want to let it wither?" Speaking to reporters on the White House South Lawn before departing for Florida, Trump said oil was passing through the Strait of Hormuz. "We are getting everything we want,” he said. He praised the US Navy for doing a “great job” of helping secure the passage of oil through the waterway and repeated his earlier claim that Hormuz was “totally ours and that’s the way we’ll keep it”.

items.title: Saudi Arabia, and the law of the sea, keeping the world’s oil moving
items.summary: Energy traders have long had a recurring nightmare. It starts with a narrow strait between Iran and Oman, through which about a fifth of the world’s oil normally passes, and ends with tankers anchored, insurers raising their rates and the price of a barrel heading north. This year, the nightmare came true. The Strait of Hormuz is largely closed, Brent is above $110 a barrel and the old question has changed. It is no longer whether Gulf oil will be disrupted but how much of it can still get out.

items.title: Egypt calls for Yemen talks as parliament weighs military support to Saudi Arabia
items.summary: Egypt calls for Yemen talks as parliament weighs military support to Saudi Arabia Egypt advocates exploring "every opportunity" to resolve the Yemen war diplomatically, its foreign minister said, ahead of a parliamentary vote next week on authorising the armed forces to support Saudi Arabia against the Iran-aligned Houthis. Any direct involvement of the Egyptian military, one of the region's largest, would raise the stakes in the fighting between the kingdom and the Houthis, an increasingly destabilising front in the spreading US-Israeli war on Iran. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi called on Saturday for an urgent parliamentary session to authorise military involvement supporting the kingdom. After a closed session on Sunday, lawmakers postponed the vote until 26 October to allow more deliberation. Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and intelligence chief Hassan Rashad travelled to Riyadh on Wednesday to deliver a letter from Sisi to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

items.title: Ahead of US and Israeli elections, 3-day joint attack on Iran 'would not radically change conflict'
items.summary: Jean-Emile Jammine is pleased to welcome Federico Donelli, Associate Professor of International Relations in the Department of Political and Social Sciences at the University of Trieste in Italy. Can another three days of military strikes achieve what eight months of confrontation have failed to deliver? Donelli challenges the assumption that a short, intensive offensive would necessarily produce a decisive political outcome. He argues, "the real question is whether military pressure is intended to constrain Iran's capacity, or to pressure Iran to sit on the table." And whether they can translate that capacity into a sustainable political outcome without provoking a wider regional crisis. Regardless, Donelli reminds us that "Iran still has leverage over the US."

items.title: The Guardian view on the Republicans’ midterms struggle: Trump has circuses, but voters also want bread | Editorial
items.summary: As prices keep rising, more of the president’s supporters are asking what happened to the economic good times he promised It is no great revelation that Donald Trump is enriching himself as president. He raked in $2.2bn in 2025, with his position and his personal interests frequently overlapping. items.title: Death toll from Houthi strike on Yemen government camp rises to 73
items.summary: Death toll from Houthi strike on Yemen government camp rises to 73 Local Yemeni authorities on Tuesday raised the death toll from a Houthi strike a day earlier on a military camp belonging to government forces to 73, as fighting between the foes escalates. It marked the deadliest attack in weeks as fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognised, Saudi-supported government rages after the collapse of a years-long truce. The death toll from Monday's strike on the camp in the energy-rich Shabwa province "increased to 73 martyrs, while search and follow-up efforts are ongoing to discover the fate of 14 missing people", authorities said in a statement. Local authorities had put the death toll at 53 on Monday, adding that more than 200 others were injured, all new members of the internal security forces who were undergoing training.

items.summary: IRGC says three tankers hit mines crossing Hormuz Strait Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Tuesday that its naval mines halted three tankers attempting to travel the Strait of Hormuz via routes considered illegal by Tehran. "Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted due to the explosion of mines planted by the brave sailors of the IRGC Navy at an illegal crossing point in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz," the IRGC said in a statement on its official Sepah News website. The Guard later said in a statement carried by state TV that a third oil tanker "exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz". The statement added that the tanker, "carrying over 2 million barrels of crude oil, had deactivated all of its radar and navigation systems".

items.title: Iran security chief rejects moving enriched uranium out of country
items.summary: Iran security chief rejects moving enriched uranium out of country Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei on Tuesday told the visiting Pakistani army chief Asim Munir that Tehran would not allow nuclear material to leave the country, according to state TV. "Not even a tiny bit of enriched nuclear material will leave Iran; such materials constitute a major asset and national wealth for the Iranian people, intended for use within the country," said Rezaei, Iran's secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. "There will be no negotiations until America takes steps to build trust - a process that must begin with the fulfilment of Iran's conditions," he added. Iran's chief negotiator and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf made similar remarks to Munir, who is in Tehran as part of a renewed push to mediate a peace deal between the Islamic Republic and the United States.

items.title: UN demands aid access to besieged Yemen city Taiz
items.summary: UN demands aid access to besieged Yemen city Taiz The United Nations insisted on Tuesday that aid must immediately be allowed to enter Yemen's Taiz, besieged by Iran-aligned Houthi fighters who are preventing supplies from reaching the country's third-largest city. Houthi fighters have encircled Taiz since early October, blocking the road that links it to Aden, interim capital of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government. "Humanitarian aid must be immediately allowed to enter the city and its passage must be facilitated," UN human rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement. He said relief must reach the city to avert a rights catastrophe. "The Houthis' closure of the only supply route linking Taiz to Aden is placing civilians at grave risk, blocking humanitarian aid and cutting off essential supplies," said Turk.

items.summary: A plurality of active-duty service members — 48% — oppose the military being used in the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, according to a poll conducted by Change Research for the advocacy group Common Defense. The poll surveyed 156 people currently serving in the military, 431 veterans, and  144 immediate family members of active-duty service members between September 15 and 28. Common Defense is a veteran-led group that advocates for progressive policies and endorses Democratic candidates, though a 47% of respondents to their September poll are self-identified Republicans. Nearly 20% identified as “pure independents,” while 35% said they were Democrats. Though Republicans surveyed in the poll backed Operation Epic Fury at a rate of 77% to 16%, overwhelming opposition among Democrats and independents left respondents opposed to the war overall, 49% to 44%. items.summary: Somewhere inside Iran, a network of activists exchanged messages about politics and news with an activist — nicknamed “Parsa” — on the messaging app Telegram. They had no idea they were actually speaking to an AI agent that had copied the real activist’s style by training it on 8,400 real Telegram posts. Instead of “Parsa,” they were actually communicating with the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran (MEK), an Iranian Islamist-Marxist opposition group widely regarded as a cult. According to a report from Anthropic released last month, this operation was carried out by four individuals working for the MEK. They built an AI agent named “Viktor” that also surveilled individuals inside Iran and flooded social media platforms with pro-MEK content under “independent” branding. The Anthropic report sheds light on how foreign actors are increasingly using artificial intelligence tools like Claude and ChatGPT for their influence operations. items.summary: Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, endured a siege from 2015 to 2017. Today, it is encircled again. The World Food Program says it cannot reach more than 600,000 people in and around the city. The International Organization for Migration counts over 200,000 people displaced since the Houthi offensive on Yemen’s Red Sea coast launched in September. Why this city, and why now? The Houthis, formally known as the Ansar Allah movement, draw their strength from the Zaydi Shia highlands of the north. Critics say their governing ideology rests on the belief that the right to rule belongs to sayyids , descendants of the Prophet Mohammad, a lineage to which the Houthi family itself belongs. The Houthis have long denied seeking to restore the Imamate, but in Taiz, which has for a decade resisted Houthi encroachment, that denial finds few believers. Taiz has a long history of political activism and hostility to the idea of religious hereditary rule. items.title: The Fog of Tech
items.summary: Mara Karlin, a defense policy expert who served as senior national-security official in multiple American administrations, makes an authoritative case that war planners tend to be overconfident about their ability to predict how new tools will shape the battlefield—blinding them to the unchanging realities of war. Using examples from Gaza, Ukraine, and Iran, Karlin shows how this "technology trap" leads to false assumptions about the future of war.

items.title: Maritime Chokepoints: Hormuz and Beyond
items.summary: Iran did not need a navy to close the Strait of Hormuz and disrupt global trade – only missiles on shore, drones in the air, and mines beneath the waves. To keep the sea lanes open, America and its allies must deter attempts to close a chokepoint and build the reserves and bypass routes that blunt the damage when narrow waterways do close.

The vessel violated Iran-imposed “regulations” by switching off its navigation system while transiting the waterway, the IRGC said. “An illicit oil tanker exploded and caught fire in its engine room after hitting a naval mine in the southern Strait of Hormuz,” the Fars news agency quoted the IRGC as saying. “If ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf switch off their navigation and identification systems, they will be dealt with severely and decisively.”

Rubio said the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia. He said various conflicts were impacting global energy prices, including the US war on Iran and attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthis. "These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other, and they're having an impact not just on global oil and diesel prices but on economies as well," he said. US lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle have sharply criticised Trump after he signed an executive order Friday that waived sweeping sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia -- measures adopted by Congress last month. items.summary: United Arab Emirates will reportedly resume payments to Yemeni forces as gains by Iran-backed Houthi fighters alarm Gulf state rulers Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved? The United Arab Emirates has agreed to re-enter the Yemen conflict by resuming payments to some government forces fighting Iran-aligned Houthis in the south, according to sources in Yemen. In return, Saudi Arabia has agreed to provide air cover for the anti-Houthi force. The new cooperation agreement is the first tangible sign that the deep rift between the UAE and Saudi Arabia over Yemen’s future is starting to be healed – if only because the advance by Houthi forces across Yemen has alarmed all the rival Gulf state rulers. items.title: Hormuz controlled by US and allies, not Iran: Centcom chief
items.summary: Hormuz controlled by US and allies, not Iran: Centcom chief The Strait of Hormuz "is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran ", the head of US Central Command (Centcom) has said. In a video statement, Centcom commander Brad Cooper said the US blockade of Iranian ports had imposed "a devastating cost" on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). He said it had completely halted Iran's maritime exports and imports, "with the exception of humanitarian assistance we have allowed in". Cooper said the US had "prevented Iran from exporting at least 25 billion dollars worth of crude oil" and had "significantly degraded Iran's ability to project power far beyond its borders". He added that US forces had helped Gulf allies ship more than 100 million barrels of crude through the strait in the past week, with around 400 merchant vessels passing through. In total, the US had helped regional partners move 1.3 billion barrels through Hormuz in recent months, he said.

items.title: La poesía no ha muerto
items.summary: Dice Andrés Trapiello que la poesía no ha muerto, esto es que vive, pero no así el mundo que la necesitaba. Lo dice, a su manera, para celebrar un aniversario de la editorial La Veleta, que el escritor fundó hace ahora cien libros de poemas, después de otras aventuras editoriales, como Trieste. Y lo celebra con la publicación de las traducciones de Emily Dickinson que debemos a Carlos Pujol, lector y traductor y persona inmejorable. Que el mundo haya necesitado la poesía alguna vez es una interesante hipótesis que muchos hechos podrían desmentir. O muchos versos: la flor que el arado destroza en el poema de Catulo, las cuatro personas para las que escribía Pound (¡oh mundo, lo siento por ti!), la tumba en el aire que excavan los judíos de la ‘Fuga de la muerte’ de Celan, o el combatiente ejecutado ante los ojos de René Char, caído como una hoja que una ráfaga de viento arrastraría... O la misma ausencia que Omar Jayyam mostró a la Luna hace mil años desde un huerto en el Jorasán iraní: ‘Cuantas y cuantas veces volverás a buscarme en el mismo jardín y todo será inútil’. items.title: Voters more worried about Iran war than immigration or crime: polls
items.summary: As election day nears, two new polls show the Iran war has emerged as one of the most important issues shaping voters’ midterm decisions. National polls from Fox News and The Associated Press-NORC place the war behind only economy-related issues, government corruption, and health care among voters’ top four concerns. Significantly, the Iran war has surpassed immigration and crime, two issues on which President Donald Trump performed particularly well in 2024, among voters’ top concerns. In the 2024 campaign, pre - and post -election polling showed those issues as ranking higher as a priority for voters than foreign policy. The Fox News survey showed 75% of respondents were either “extremely” (42%) or “very” (33%) concerned about the war in Iran. According to the AP-NORC poll , 62% of registered voters named the war as one of the most important issues, and a further 31% said it was “an important issue, but not one of the most important.” The Fox poll further found that six in 10 voters oppose U.S. military action against Iran, and those voters favor Democratic congressional candidates

items.summary: UN Security Council condemns 'escalatory' Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia The UN Security Council has condemned the "escalatory" attacks by Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi Arabia, including "reckless strikes" on Riyadh's airport. The Saudi capital's international airport has been targeted by strikes 20 times since the beginning of the month, with an attack last weekend killing 13 people and wounding more than 300. In a joint statement shared by the Security Council's president, Greece's Evangelos Sekeris, the 15-member UN body also condemned "continued Houthi attacks and threats against commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab (Strait)". The statement also "affirmed the inherent right of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia of self-defence in accordance with international law."

items.title: Gulf states have downplayed damage caused by Iranian strikes: Report
items.summary: Gulf states have downplayed damage caused by Iranian strikes: Report Arabian Gulf monarchies have “suppressed” information about the extent of damage done to their physical infrastructure by attacks from Iran and its allies, Reuters reported on Thursday. Gulf states such as Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, and Kuwait faced thousands of missile and drone strikes launched by Iran in retaliation for the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic on 28 February. More recently, Saudi Arabia has come under attack from the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthis and Iran targeted civilian infrastructure like pipelines, energy facilities and, in one case, a nuclear energy plant. Reuters' assessment is likely to cast new doubt on how Gulf states describe strikes on their territories. For example, Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said that a Houthi drone strike caused a "limited fire" at the headquarters of the kingdom's national oil company, Aramco, in Dhahran. Iran’s deputy legal affairs minister called for Israel to be expelled from CICA following Herzog's speech in Baku. Kazem Gharibabadi was quoted as saying by Iran's IRIB news that “sustainable security” in Asia was not achieved through “threats and pressure, but through mutual respect, trust-building and equal cooperation among independent states”. “If the international community does not stop America and Israel today, their aggression will spread to all independent countries. items.summary: Chinese refiners rush to buy Middle East crude as stocks fall, Kpler says Chinese refiners are stepping up purchases of Middle Eastern crude as record inventory drawdowns and a recovery in refinery activity boost demand for prompt cargoes, according to analytics firm Kpler. Chinese buyers have secured at least 80 million barrels of Saudi crude since mid-September, Kpler said on X. China’s onshore crude inventories fell by about 1.6 million barrels per day in September, the fastest pace on record. Refinery throughput is projected to reach 14.2 million barrels per day by December, adding to pressure on refiners to rebuild stocks. At the same time, Chinese refiners need to replace roughly 1 million barrels per day of Iranian supply, with the US blockade still in place, according to Kpler. Stronger Chinese demand could limit further weakness in Dubai crude pricing, particularly as escalating regional tensions continue to threaten supply flows.

items.title: Overthrowing Iran's government 'essential for Israel's security', Netanyahu says
items.summary: Overthrowing Iran's government 'essential for Israel's security', Netanyahu says Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says that although overthrowing Iran’s government "remains essential for Israel's security", it is unlikely to happen before Israel’s elections on 27 October. “No, I don’t think that’s realistic,” he said in an interview with Israeli public broadcaster Kan. “We have done a great deal. We have crushed it. They are at their weakest point, but we need to finish the job,” he said. He accused political rivals Gadi Eisenkot and Yair Golan of opposing efforts to overthrow Iran’s government, insisting that its removal was necessary for Israel’s security. Netanyahu claimed that Israeli military operations against Iran had prevented it from acquiring nuclear weapons.

items.title: Houthi strikes mark the end of Saudi Arabia's Yemen 'containment strategy'
items.summary: Houthi strikes mark the end of Saudi Arabia's Yemen 'containment strategy' Saudi Arabia ’s bid to “contain” the Houthis in Yemen while doubling down on economic growth at home is collapsing, posing one of the most serious tests for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman since he rose to power, according to analysts and diplomats. A decade ago, the crown prince led the kingdom into a war aimed at ousting the Houthis from power. The conflict turned into a quagmire for Saudi Arabia, sapping its resources and sparking widespread backlash due to its devastating bombing campaign. In the end, Saudi Arabia cut its losses and maintained an uneasy truce with the Houthis since 2022. “This is the collapse of Saudi Arabia’s containment strategy,” Rob Geist Pinfold, an international security expert at King's College London, told Middle East Eye. “The way Saudi Arabia approached the Houthis in the last few years was not dissimilar to how Israel treated Hamas in Gaza before 7 October [2023]. items.title: Twee schepen gezonken in Straat van Hormuz in de afgelopen 24 uur
items.summary: Een containerschip en een bulkschip zijn het afgelopen etmaal gezonken nadat ze in of bij de Straat van Hormuz door projectielen waren geraakt, zeggen maritieme diensten. Het is niet bekend of de schepen zijn geraakt door projectielen van Iran. Dat land heeft het aantal aanvallen in de zeestraat deze maand opgevoerd . Het kleine containerschip GFS Pride dat onder Singaporese vlag voer, zonk toen het gisteren tijdens de doorvaart door de zeestraat werd geraakt. Op het schip brak brand uit, meldt de maritieme dienst van Singapore. Niemand raakte gewond, de 21 bemanningsleden zijn geëvacueerd. Het tweede schip Cape Dao, dat onder de vlag van Antigua en Barbuda voer, zonk in de buurt van Oman. Dat schip werd al op 23 september door een projectiel geraakt. Een bemanningslid kwam toen om het leven. De andere opvarenden werden volgens maritieme bronnen direct na de inslag geëvacueerd. De Iraanse staatstelevisie heeft beelden getoond van beide schepen: Dat schepen zinken na een aanval in de zeestraat is zeldzaam.
